questions.q: A Bloom filter lookup returns 'no'. What do you know?
options: The element was deleted at some point earlier
The element is definitely not in the set
The element is probably absent, with some error chance
Nothing; negative results are unreliable by design
questions.explanation: Any inserted element has all k of its bits set, so a single zero bit proves it was never inserted. Negatives are exact; only positives carry uncertainty.

questions.q: A Bloom filter lookup returns 'yes'. What do you know?
options: The element is certainly present in the set
The element was inserted exactly once, never more
The element may be present, or this may be a false positive
The element's hash collided, so the filter needs resizing
questions.explanation: All k bits being set may simply mean other elements happened to set them collectively. The filter never stores keys, so it cannot distinguish a real hit from a collision.

questions.q: What happens inside a Bloom filter on insert?
options: k hash functions each set one bit in the bit array
The element is appended to a compressed list
One hash selects a bucket that stores the element's key
The bit array is rehashed to include the new element
questions.explanation: Insertion hashes the element k ways into positions in the bit array and sets each of those bits to 1. Nothing about the element itself is retained.

questions.q: Why can't a standard Bloom filter support deletion?
options: Deletion requires re-presenting the original element, which the filter never stored
The bit array is write-once hardware in most implementations
Deletes would leave tombstones that break the hashing
Clearing a bit may also 'remove' other elements that share that bit
questions.explanation: Bits are shared across elements, so zeroing one element's bits can silently erase another element's evidence, introducing false negatives that destroy the filter's core guarantee.

questions.q: What two parameters chiefly determine a Bloom filter's false-positive rate?
options: Bits per element and the number of hash functions
The CPU speed and the array's memory bandwidth
Element size in bytes and the compression codec used
Insertion order and the seed of the first hash
questions.explanation: The error rate follows from m/n (bits per element) and k (hash count) alone. The size of the elements themselves is irrelevant, since only their hashes are used.

questions.q: Why are Bloom filters so memory-efficient compared to hash sets?
options: They compress the stored keys with entropy coding
They store only bit patterns, never the elements or their keys
They deduplicate elements before storing them
They keep the actual data on disk, using RAM only for a small index
questions.explanation: A hash set must retain every key for exact comparison; a Bloom filter keeps only a handful of bits per element. That is precisely what it trades for false positives.

questions.q: As more elements are inserted into a fixed-size Bloom filter, what happens?
options: Lookups slow down linearly with the element count
The filter rejects inserts once 50% of bits are set
False negatives begin appearing alongside false positives
The false-positive rate climbs as more bits are set
questions.explanation: More insertions mean more 1 bits, so random probes are increasingly likely to hit all-ones by chance. Lookup cost stays O(k); only accuracy degrades.

questions.q: Which is a classic Bloom filter use case?
options: Storing user passwords in a compact but fully recoverable form
Ordering events across distributed nodes
Skipping disk lookups for keys an SSTable definitely lacks
Load balancing requests across identical replicas
questions.explanation: LSM-tree stores keep a per-SSTable filter so a definite 'no' skips the disk read entirely. It fits the pattern: cheap in-memory check guarding an expensive operation.

questions.q: A web crawler uses a Bloom filter for 'have I seen this URL?'. What is the practical consequence of a false positive?
options: The same URL ends up crawled twice, wasting bandwidth and storage
The crawler crashes on the unrecognized URL
A never-visited URL is skipped and may never be crawled
The filter must be rebuilt from the frontier queue
questions.explanation: A false positive reports 'already seen' for a fresh URL, so the crawler skips it and loses that page. Duplicate crawling would require false negatives, which cannot occur.

questions.q: Roughly how much memory does a Bloom filter need for a 1% false-positive rate?
options: About 1 bit per element regardless of target rate
About 32 bytes per element, matching the size of each hash output
It depends only on element size, not element count
Roughly 10 bits per element, independent of element size
questions.explanation: Roughly 9.6 bits per element yields 1% error, and each additional ~4.8 bits cuts the rate tenfold. Element byte size never enters the formula.

questions.q: Given a fixed bit array, what does using too many hash functions cause?
options: Hash collisions corrupt the array's structure
Bits saturate faster, raising the false-positive rate despite more checks
Lookups start returning false negatives under load
Standard implementations silently ignore all hash functions beyond the optimal count
questions.explanation: Each extra hash sets another bit per insert, so the array fills toward all-ones sooner. Past the optimum, that saturation outweighs the benefit of requiring more bits to match.

questions.q: How does a counting Bloom filter enable deletion?
options: Each position holds a small counter, incremented on insert and decremented on delete
It stores each element's full key beside its bits
It keeps an append-only log of every insert so deletes can replay the log backward
It partitions the array per element, isolating their bits
questions.explanation: Counters instead of single bits track how many elements set each slot, so a decrement removes one element without erasing others. The cost is several bits per slot.

questions.q: Why do databases place Bloom filters in front of on-disk structures like SSTables?
options: The filter caches the hottest key-value pairs in RAM for instant reads
Filters re-sort the SSTable for faster binary search
Disk blocks are verified against the filter for corruption
A cheap RAM check avoids most pointless disk reads for absent keys
questions.explanation: Most lookups in an LSM tree miss most SSTables. A definite 'not present' from RAM eliminates that I/O, which dominates the cost of a read.

questions.q: One-hit-wonder URLs make a CDN cache objects nobody requests twice. How does a Bloom filter help?
options: It predicts future popularity from the URL's structure
It compresses one-hit objects so caching them is free
Cache only on the second request: the filter remembers first-time URLs cheaply
It evicts unpopular cached objects by scanning the whole cache every night
questions.explanation: The filter tracks 'seen once' for a tiny fraction of the memory a URL set would need, so objects only enter the cache after a second request proves some reuse.

questions.q: An email service checks incoming addresses against 10M known-spam senders on every message. Why is a Bloom filter attractive?
options: The whole set fits in a few dozen megabytes of RAM with tiny lookup cost
It guarantees genuine spam is never misclassified as legitimate correspondence
It updates itself as spammers change addresses
It hides the spam list's contents from subpoenas
questions.explanation: At about 10 bits per entry, 10M senders need roughly 12 MB, and each check is a few hash computations. Storing the addresses themselves would cost far more.

questions.q: A Bloom filter screens senders against a spam list. What does a false positive cause?
options: A spam message slips through unfiltered
A legitimate sender is treated as if on the spam list
The message gets duplicated into both quarantine and the inbox simultaneously
The filter must rebuild before more mail flows
questions.explanation: The filter wrongly reports membership, so an innocent address is flagged as spam. Real spam slipping through would need a false negative, which Bloom filters never produce.

questions.q: You sized a Bloom filter for 10M elements at 1% FP, but 40M arrive. Rough effect on the false-positive rate?
options: It stays near 1%, since the rate depends only on hash count
It degrades dramatically, plausibly past 30%, as the array saturates
It rises precisely linearly, landing at exactly 4% for four times the elements
It becomes 100% the moment capacity is doubled
questions.explanation: False-positive rate grows roughly exponentially in n for fixed m, not linearly. At 4x the planned load the bit array is heavily saturated and accuracy collapses.

questions.q: Optimal hash count k for m bits and n elements is (m/n) times ln 2. What does this optimum actually balance?
options: Setting enough bits to discriminate versus saturating the array with 1s
The CPU cost of computing hashes versus available memory bandwidth per query
The array's length versus its width
Collision resistance versus preimage resistance
questions.explanation: More hashes make an accidental match require more coincidences, but also fill the array faster. The optimum lands where about half the bits are set.

questions.q: A distributed cache shares one Bloom filter across nodes, and entries expire hourly. Core difficulty?
options: Standard Bloom filters cannot be serialized for transfer across the network
Hash functions differ across CPU architectures
Expired entries cannot be cleared, so the filter's error grows until rebuilt
The filter must be locked globally for every read
questions.explanation: Without deletion, expired keys keep their bits set forever, so the filter monotonically fills and its error climbs. Practical fixes are periodic rebuilds or rotating generational filters.

questions.q: Compared to a Bloom filter at equal FP rate, what does a cuckoo filter additionally offer?
options: A guarantee of zero false positives while the load factor stays below one half
Range queries over the stored fingerprints
Cryptographic tamper evidence for its contents
Deletion support and often better space efficiency at low FP rates
questions.explanation: Cuckoo filters store per-item fingerprints in buckets, so an item can be located and removed, and below roughly 3% error they beat Bloom filters on space too.
